To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 3 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .05 Figure 1: Correlation matrix showing Kendall’s tau between mood regulation strategies, efficacy measures, and hope and subscales agency and pathway (p < .05).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 185 columns across 2 data files.

Issues Identified

7 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

136 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 17 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 2 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 MS2_Results.qmd — numeric
2 MS2_Supplementary_Material.qmd — numeric

File paths

3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: C:\\Users\\dancroro\\OneDrive - Jyväskylän yliopisto\\Music and climate\\MusicAndClimateChang_DATA_2026-01-15_All_instruments.csv to MusicAndClimateChang_DATA_2026-01-15_All_instruments.csv (in MS2_Results.qmd); C:\\Users\\dancroro\\OneDrive - Jyväskylän yliopisto\\Music and climate\\MusicAndClimateChange_DataDictionary_2026_01_15.csv to MusicAndClimateChange_DataDictionary_2026_01_15.csv (in MS2_Results.qmd); C:\\Users\\dancroro\\OneDrive - Jyväskylän yliopisto\\Music and climate\\MusicAndClimateChange_DataDictionary_2026_01_15.csv to MusicAndClimateChange_DataDictionary_2026_01_15.csv (in MS2_Supplementary_Material.qmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

> ref_countries <- countrycode::codelist$country.name.en %>% unique() %>% na.omit()
> ref_norm <- norm_nat(ref_countries)
> ref_tbl <- tibble::tibble(country_raw = ref_countries, country_norm = ref_norm)
> closest_country <- function(x_norm, max_dist = 2) {
>   # Compute distances to all reference normalized names
>   d <- utils::adist(x_norm, ref_tbl$country_norm, partial = FALSE, ignore.case = FALSE)
>   min_idx <- which.min(d)
>   min_dist <- d[min_idx]
> 
>   if (length(min_idx) == 0 || is.infinite(min_dist) || min_dist > max_dist) {
>     return(NA_character_)
>   } else {
>     return(ref_tbl$country_raw[min_idx])
>   }
> }
> map_nationality <- function(x) {
>   x_clean <- norm_nat(x)
> 
>   # 5a) Custom regex dictionary (high precision for common messy cases)
>   hit <- demonym_dict %>%
>     filter(stringr::str_detect(x_clean, pattern)) %>%
>     slice(1) %>%
>     pull(country_name)
> 
>   # 5b) If not hit, try countrycode name resolution (on raw and cleaned)
>   if (length(hit) == 0 || is.na(hit)) {
>     try_names <- c(x, x_clean)
>     cc_try <- purrr::map_chr(
>       try_names,
>       ~ suppressWarnings(countrycode::countryname(.x, destination = "country.name.en"))
>     )
>     hit <- cc_try[!is.na(cc_try)][1]
>     if (length(hit) == 0) hit <- NA_character_
>   }
> 
>   # 5c) Fuzzy fallback via adist if still missing
>   if (is.na(hit)) {
>     cand <- closest_country(x_clean, max_dist = 2)
>     # Optional: require very close match (e.g., <=1) to reduce false positives
>     hit <- cand
>   }
> 
>   iso3 <- if (!is.na(hit)) countrycode::countrycode(hit, "country.name.en", "iso3c") else NA_character_
> 
>   tibble::tibble(
>     input   = x,
>     cleaned = x_clean,
>     country = hit,
>     iso3c   = iso3
>   )
> }
> map_nationalities <- function(x_vec) {
>   purrr::map_dfr(x_vec, map_nationality)
> }

> label_un_development <- function(iso3c,
>                                  developed_label = "Developed",
>                                  developing_label = "Developing",
>                                  developed_overrides = character(),
>                                  developing_overrides = character()) {
>   # Pull UN region info
>   un_map <- countrycode::codelist %>%
>     select(iso3c, country.name.en, un.region.name, un.regionsub.name) %>% 
>     distinct()
> 
>   developed_iso3c <- un_map %>%
>     mutate(dev = case_when(
>       # Explicit overrides first
>       iso3c %in% developed_overrides ~ TRUE,
>       iso3c %in% developing_overrides ~ FALSE,
>       # UN M49 convention
>       un.region.name == "Europe" ~ TRUE,
>       un.regionsub.name == "Northern America" ~ TRUE,
>       iso3c %in% c("JPN", "AUS", "NZL") ~ TRUE,
>       TRUE ~ FALSE
>     )) %>%
>     transmute(iso3c, dev)
>   
>    # Collapse to one row per iso3c to avoid join duplication
>   map1 <- developed_iso3c %>%
>     group_by(iso3c) %>%
>     summarise(
>       dev = {
>         vals <- dev
>         if (all(is.na(vals))) NA
>         else any(vals, na.rm = TRUE)
>       },
>       .groups = "drop"
>     )
> 
>   tibble::tibble(iso3c = iso3c) %>%
>     left_join(map1, by = "iso3c") %>%
>     mutate(
>       un_dev_label = case_when(
>         is.na(dev) ~ NA_character_,             # unknown code or not in codelist
>         dev ~ developed_label,
>         TRUE ~ developing_label
>       )
>     ) %>%
>     pull(un_dev_label)
> }

> model <- '
>   # MEASUREMENT MODEL
>   
>   # B-MMR Brief Music for Mood Regulation
>   Entertainment =~ bmmr_2 + bmmr_10 + bmmr_21 
>   Revival =~ bmmr_11 + bmmr_14 + bmmr_17
>   Strong_Sensation =~ bmmr_7 + bmmr_9 + bmmr_12
>   Diversion =~ bmmr_4 + bmmr_5 + bmmr_20 
>   Discharge =~  bmmr_6 + bmmr_3 + bmmr_13 
>   Mental_Work =~ bmmr_15 + bmmr_19 + bmmr_18 
>   Solace =~ bmmr_1 + bmmr_8 + bmmr_16
>   
>   BMMR =~ Entertainment +
>      Revival +
>      Strong_Sensation +
>      Diversion +
>      Discharge +
>      Mental_Work +
>      Solace
> 
>   # allow residual covariance for similar items
>   bmmr_6  ~~  bmmr_13
>   
>   # Hope scale
>   Hope =~ ahs_2 + ahs_9 + ahs_10 + ahs_1 + ahs_4 + ahs_6 + ahs_8 + ahs_12
>   
>   # allow residual covariance for similar items
>   ahs_12  ~~  ahs_8
>   
>   # STRUCTURAL MODEL
>   # Paths from BMMR to observed mediators
>   self_eff      ~ a1*BMMR
>   outc_exp      ~ a2*BMMR
>   coll_eff      ~ a3*BMMR
>   coll_outc_exp ~ a4*BMMR
>   
>   # Example outcome model using latent Hope
>   Hope ~ b1*self_eff +
>          b2*outc_exp +
>          b3*coll_eff +
>          b4*coll_outc_exp +
>          cprime*BMMR
>          
>   # Correlated residuals among mediators, if theoretically appropriate
>   self_eff ~~ outc_exp + coll_eff + coll_outc_exp
>   outc_exp ~~ coll_eff + coll_outc_exp
>   coll_eff ~~ coll_outc_exp
>   
>   # Specific indirect effects
>   ind_self_eff      := a1*b1
>   ind_outc_exp      := a2*b2
>   ind_coll_eff      := a3*b3
>   ind_coll_outc_exp := a4*b4
>   
>   # Aggregate effects
>   total_indirect := ind_self_eff + ind_outc_exp +
>                     ind_coll_eff + ind_coll_outc_exp
>   direct := cprime
>   total := cprime + total_indirect
>   '
> SEM_wlsmv <- sem(model,

> )

> library(lavaan)
> library(semTools)
> library(ggplot2)
> set.seed(2026)
> mc <- monteCarloCI(SEM_wlsmv, nRep = 100000, standardized = TRUE)
> mc_df <- as.data.frame(mc)
> names(mc_df)[1:3] <- c("est", "lo", "hi")
> mc_df$param <- rownames(mc_df)
> mc_txt <- function(p, d = 3) {
>   r <- mc_df[mc_df$param == p, ]
>   sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f [%.", d, "f, %.", d, "f]"), r$est, r$lo, r$hi)
> }
> mc_sig <- function(p) {
>   r <- mc_df[mc_df$param == p, ]
>   ifelse(r$lo > 0 | r$hi < 0, "*", "")      # CI excludes 0
> }
> std   <- standardizedSolution(SEM_wlsmv)
> stars <- function(p) as.character(cut(p, c(-Inf, .001, .01, .05, Inf),
>                                       c("***", "**", "*", "")))
> get_reg <- function(lhs, rhs) std[std$op == "~" & std$lhs == lhs & std$rhs == rhs, ]
> fmt     <- function(r) sprintf("%.2f%s", r$est.std, stars(r$pvalue))
> meds <- data.frame(
>   var   = c("self_eff", "outc_exp", "coll_eff", "coll_outc_exp"),
>   label = c("Self-efficacy", "Outcome expectancy",
>             "Collective efficacy", "Coll. outcome expect."),
>   ind   = c("ind_self_eff", "ind_outc_exp", "ind_coll_eff", "ind_coll_outc_exp"),
>   y     = c(3, 2, 1, 0),
>   stringsAsFactors = FALSE
> )
> for (i in seq_len(nrow(meds))) {
>   meds$a_lab[i]   <- fmt(get_reg(meds$var[i], "BMMR"))
>   meds$b_lab[i]   <- fmt(get_reg("Hope", meds$var[i]))
>   meds$box_lab[i] <- sprintf("%s\nindirect = %s%s\n95%% MC CI [%.3f, %.3f]",
>                              meds$label[i],
>                              sprintf("%.3f", mc_df$est[mc_df$param == meds$ind[i]]),
>                              mc_sig(meds$ind[i]),
>                              mc_df$lo[mc_df$param == meds$ind[i]],
>                              mc_df$hi[mc_df$param == meds$ind[i]])
> }
> direct <- get_reg("Hope", "BMMR")
> xB <- 0
> xM <- 4.5
> xH <- 9
> yC <- 1.5
> p <- ggplot() +
>   # a paths
>   geom_segment(data = meds, aes(x = xB + .6, y = yC, xend = xM - 1.3, yend = y),
>                arrow = arrow(length = unit(.15, "cm"))) +
>   # b paths
>   geom_segment(data = meds, aes(x = xM + 1.3, y = y, xend = xH - .6, yend = yC),
>                arrow = arrow(length = unit(.15, "cm"))) +
>   # direct path c', routed below the mediators
>   geom_path(data = data.frame(x = c(xB, xB, xH, xH),
>                               y = c(yC - .3, -1.3, -1.3, yC - .3)),
>             aes(x, y), arrow = arrow(length = unit(.15, "cm"))) +
>   annotate("label", x = (xB + xH) / 2, y = -1,  size = 3.8,
>            label = sprintf("Direct c' = %.2f%s, 95%% MC CI [%.3f, %.3f]",
>                            direct$est.std, stars(direct$pvalue),
>                            mc_df$lo[mc_df$param == "direct"],
>                            mc_df$hi[mc_df$param == "direct"])) +
>   # path coefficient labels
>   geom_label(data = meds,
>              aes(x = xB + .6 + .35 * (xM - 1.9 - xB),
>                  y = yC + .35 * (y - yC), label = a_lab),
>               size = 3.5, fill = "white") +
>   geom_label(data = meds,
>              aes(x = xH - .6 - .35 * (xH - 1.9 - xM),
>                  y = yC + .35 * (y - yC), label = b_lab),
>              size = 3.5, fill = "white") +
>   # nodes
>   geom_label(data = meds, aes(xM, y, label = box_lab), fill = "#E1F5EE", size = 3.6) +
>   annotate("label", x = xB, y = yC, label = "BMMR", fill = "#EEEDFE", size = 5) +
>   annotate("label", x = xH, y = yC, label = "Hope", fill = "#EEEDFE", size = 5) +
>   # summary text
>   annotate("text", x = (xB + xH) / 2, y = 4.2, size = 3.6,
>            label = sprintf(paste0("Total indirect = %s;  total = %s\n",
>                                   "(standardized; Monte Carlo CIs, 100,000 draws; ",
>                                   "* = CI excludes 0)"),
>                            mc_txt("total_indirect"), mc_txt("total"))) +
>   xlim(-1, 10) + theme_void()
> p
> ggsave("MS2_mediation_sem.png", p, width = 11, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)
> eff_tab <- data.frame(
>   Effect = c(meds$label, "Total indirect", "Direct (c')", "Total"),
>   Param  = c(meds$ind, "total_indirect", "direct", "total")
> )
> eff_tab$beta <- sapply(eff_tab$Param, function(p) {
>   est <- mc_df$est[mc_df$param == p]
>   sprintf("%.3f%s", est, mc_sig(p))
> })
> eff_tab$CI_95_MC <- sapply(eff_tab$Param, function(p) {
>   sprintf(
>     "[%.3f, %.3f]",
>     mc_df$lo[mc_df$param == p],
>     mc_df$hi[mc_df$param == p]
>   )
> })
> eff_tab$Param <- NULL

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants provided electronic informed consent before accessing the survey.

Recruitment occurred in two phases: roughly one-third of respondents were reached through mailing lists and social media, while the remaining participants were later recruited through the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/).

Individuals recruited via Prolific received financial compensation at a rate of £9 per hour, adjusted to the actual survey duration.

Analyses were conducted using the R Statistical language (version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2025) on Windows 11 x64 (build 26200 Participants 366 participants filled the survey at least partially. 1 participant reported being under the age of legal consent (15) and was excluded. 52 participants were missing all responses to the B-MMR scale, efficacy items, and hope scale and were excluded.

Participants had 42 unique nationalities and resided in 38 unique countries. 197 were from developed countries (Europe, North America, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Israel), and 112 were from developing countries.

Third, the adapted measure of music-based mood regulation referred broadly to climate-related emotions, a category that spans diverse positive and negative states; however, we did not assess which specific emotions participants were regulating (e.g., anger, anxiety, worry, hope), nor did we capture contextual features of musical engagement (e.g., listening situations, genre, or mode of interaction).

Ethics approval statement:

In line with the Finnish National Board on Research Integrity (TENK) guidelines for ethical review in human sciences (https://tenk.fi/sites/default/files/2021-01/Ethical_review_in_human_sciences_2020.pdf), the study did not require formal ethics approval due to its minimal-risk nature.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
