We checked 40 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the FLoRA database were found.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Climate change is associated with a range of emotional responses, yet little is known about the role of music in regulating climate-related emotions and supporting adaptive psychological outcomes. Because music is widely used to regulate emotions and can foster positive affect, emotional coping, and resilience, it may also help individuals maintain hope when confronting the challenges of climate change. The present study examined whether music-based mood regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope, and whether this relationship is mediated by climate efficacy beliefs. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 310 adults. Participants reported their use of music to regulate climaterelated emotions, climate efficacy beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, collective efficacy, and collective outcome expectancy), and hope. Relationships among the variables were examined using correlation analyses and structural equation modeling. Several musicbased regulation strategies, particularly solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival, were positively associated with hope. Some regulation strategies were also positively associated with self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, and collective outcome expectancy, whereas no significant bivariate associations emerged with collective efficacy. Structural equation modeling indicated a significant total indirect effect of music-based regulation on hope through climate efficacy beliefs. However, only self-efficacy and collective efficacy emerged as significant mediators. Outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy did not significantly mediate the association. The direct association between music-based regulation and hope remained significant, indicating partial mediation. These findings suggest that individuals who use music to regulate climate-related emotions report greater hope and that this association is partly explained by stronger perceptions of personal and collective capability. Climate efficacy beliefs emerged as a small yet significant pathway linking music-based regulation and hope. Music may therefore represent an accessible everyday resource that supports adaptive engagement with climate emotions and fosters hope in the context of climate change.

Introduction

The climate crisis increasingly shapes the texture of our daily emotional life, functioning not only as an environmental emergency but also as a profound psychological context (Doherty & Clayton, 2011). As people encounter rising temperatures, extreme weather events and ecological degradation, they also experience a growing set of climate emotions that reflect both personal concern and broader existential threat, including eco-anxiety, eco-grief or eco-guilt (Pihkala, 2022). While these emotions can be challenging, they may also motivate engagement with environmental issues and climate action (Ogunbode et al., 2022). An important factor that may shape whether individuals remain constructively engaged is hope. Hope is a multifaceted psychological construct frequently defined as a cognitivemotivational state comprising agency (goal-directed determination) and pathways (planning to meet goals) (Snyder et al., 1991). Recently, hope has been proposed as an antidote for eco-emotions and earth-related mental challenges (Laranjeira et al., 2024). Since how we perceive the future can hugely affect how we feel in the present, decades of positive psychology research has shown substantial associations of hope with subjective, psychological and social wellbeing (Murphy, 2023). Within the broaden-and-build theory (Fredricksonhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XzQQis 2001) , hope functions as a positive emotion that widens individuals' momentary perspectives and action repertoire, and supports the development of psychological resources to deal with stressful situations. In the climate context, hope may therefore help individuals maintain resilience, cope with uncertainty, and sustain long-term engagement with climate action (Pihkala, 2018).

Given the importance of hope for psychological adaptation and sustained engagement in the climate crisis, it becomes increasingly important to understand how people regulate their climate emotions in everyday life (Ortner et al., 2025). Climate emotions often arise unpredictably (e.g., through news exposure, weather anomalies, conversations, or personal reflections) and their intensity can fluctuate across daily contexts (Alabak & Verduyn, 2025). Without effective regulation, these emotions may accumulate and contribute to heightened distress, rumination, or paralysis; conversely, when individuals are able to process and integrate their feelings, they are more likely to sustain constructive engagement and maintain a sense of hope (Alabak & Verduyn, 2025; Ibrahim, 2024). For instance, recent experimental work shows that specific emotion-regulation strategies used in response to climate information can meaningfully alter emotional outcomes, such as reducing negative affect or increasing hope, and, in some cases, shape intentions to engage in climate-mitigating actions (Armstrong et al., 2025). Everyday regulatory practices therefore play a crucial role in determining whether climate emotions become overwhelming or instead support adaptive coping, resilience, and future-oriented motivation.

Music Engagement as Everyday Affective Regulation

Listening to music is one of the most widely used tools for affect regulation in everyday life (van Goethem & Sloboda, 2011). People turn to music across a wide range of situations from managing daily stress to navigating complex emotional experiences, because it is easily accessible, socially embedded, and capable of eliciting rapid shifts in physiological arousal, mood, and meaning (Feneberg et al., 2025). Music thus offers both immediate emotional modulation and deeper opportunities for reflection, expression, and coping, making it a versatile resource for regulating affect in everyday contexts. Established models of music-based mood regulation (Saarikallio, 2012) show that people draw on diverse strategies (entertainment, revival, strong sensation, diversion, discharge, mental work, and solace) to manage, express, or transform emotional states in daily life. The accessawareness-agency (AAA) model (Saarikallio, 2019) conceptualizes this process as the interplay of embodied access to emotional experience, reflective awareness of that experience, and a resulting sense of agency in shaping one's affective state. These components are particularly relevant for climate emotions, which are often morally complex, ambiguous, and intense, making them likely candidates for regulation through music. Through embodied access, music can help individuals contact and articulate difficult climate-related feelings; through reflective awareness, it can support meaning-making and emotional clarity; and through agency, it may foster a sense of empowerment in the face of climate threats.

These processes suggest that music may help individuals process, contain, or reframe climate-related emotions in ways that influence their broader psychological functioning. Accordingly, music and arts-based practices have been highlighted as vital pathways for individuals to work through climate emotions, manage stress and foster hope and resilience (Ibrahim, 2024). Music, with its unique ability to entrain physiological rhythms and evoke complex emotional responses, has emerged as a potent medium for fostering hope, especially within music therapy and music medicine research (Wilson, 2025). By providing a safe haven for emotional expression and playful creativity, music helps individuals reconnect with their empowered selves and envision a meaningful future (Bennett et al., 2024). Particularly in mental health and psychiatric care as well as oncology and palliative care, music interventions have shown significant improvements in hope and happiness (Jethva et al., 2025; Silverman, 2016). Importantly, the hope-enhancing potential of music is not limited to clinical populations, as music listening in experiments has been found to increase self-reported hope among healthy adults (Gupta & Gupta, 2016; Ziv et al., 2011). However, how music-based regulation of climate emotions relates to hope in climate contexts has received no academic attention so far. Moreover, the psychological mechanisms through which such regulation might exert its effects, including potential pathways such as cognitive processes, remain largely underexplored.

Climate-Efficacy Beliefs as Psychological Mechanisms

Building on Social Cognitive Theory (Bandurahttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?CPCT5T 1986) , climate-efficacy beliefs represent core cognitive appraisals that shape how individuals interpret and respond to the climate crisis (Koletsou & Mancy, 2011). Self-efficacy and collective efficacy beliefs capture the extent to which individuals feel personally capable of contributing to climate solutions and perceive groups as capable of acting effectively (Choi & Hart, 2021). In parallel, outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy beliefs reflect whether people expect their own actions and coordinated collective efforts to produce meaningful environmental outcomes (Choi & Hart, 2021). A large body of research shows that these beliefs reliably predict climate change attitudeshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?pVC2el mitigation intentions, climate policy support and pro-environmental behavior (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?pVC2el Choi & Hart, 2021; Hanss et al., 2025; Hurst Loo & Walker, 2023) , suggesting that feeling capable of influencing outcomes is a central driver of environmental views and action. Furthermore, studies of high school students have identified perceived personal competence and trust in collective action as key predictors of hope in the context of climate change (Li & Monroe, 2019). Especially constructive hopehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?iJty6M rooted in meaning-making, trust and positive reappraisal instead of denial, appears to be particularly relevant for climate engagement (Ojala, 2012) , highlighting the importance of strategies that help individuals navigate and transform their emotional responses to climate change. Efficacy and outcome expectancy beliefs have also been studied extensively in health and wellbeing research, showing substantial benefits for mental and physical health (Brown et al., 2014; Lo et al., 2023). Consequently, researchers have increasingly examined self-and collective efficacy beliefs as a key cognitive mechanism in the psychological adaptation to the climate crisis (Hurst Loo & Walker, 2023).

Given this central role of efficacy beliefs in shaping both environmental action and emotional functioning, it is plausible that they also serve as a mechanism linking music-based regulation of climate emotions to wellbeing. Regulating emotions through music-whether by gaining emotional clarity, expressing difficult feelings, or shifting one's perspective-may help individuals move from overwhelm toward a more coherent sense of agency (Saarikallio et al., 2020). Based on the access-awareness-agency model (Saarikalliohttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?cs7gx8 2019) , such regulatory experiences through music can support the formation of stronger efficacy beliefs by fostering feelings of capability and empowerment. For example, recent research shows that identifying strongly as a music person affects mental health only indirectly, because it boosts a person's self-efficacy, which in turn supports better wellbeing (Koehler et al., 2026). At the same time, music-based meaning-making (e.g., through climate-themed lyrics) or connection with others through music (e.g., engaging with activist artists) may enhance outcome expectancy beliefs, reinforcing the perception that individual and collective efforts can produce meaningful environmental change. Music-based regulation may therefore influence wellbeing partly through its impact on these core cognitive appraisals.

Research questions

The present study aims to examine whether music-based regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope in the climate crisis, and whether these associations operate through climate-efficacy beliefs. Building on research showing that music is a powerful tool for affect regulation and that efficacy-related cognitions are central to emotional resilience and climate engagement, the study proposes that music-based regulation may shape how capable and effective individuals feel in responding to climate change. These efficacy beliefs, in turn, are expected to influence whether people experience greater hope. We formulated the following hypotheses: H1 (Hope): Higher levels of music-based regulation of climate emotions are associated with higher hope.

H2 (Efficacy beliefs):

Higher levels of music-based regulation of climate emotions are associated with stronger climate-efficacy beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, collective efficacy, collective outcome expectancy).

H3 (Mediation):

The associations between music-based regulation and higher hope are mediated by stronger climate-efficacy beliefs.

Methods Procedure

This cross-sectional study was carried out between May 2025 and January 2026 using an online questionnaire administered via REDCap, which required 15 minutes to complete. Participants provided electronic informed consent before accessing the survey. Recruitment occurred in two phases: roughly one-third of respondents were reached through mailing lists and social media, while the remaining participants were later recruited through the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/). Individuals recruited via Prolific received financial compensation at a rate of £9 per hour, adjusted to the actual survey duration. In line with the Finnish National Board on Research Integrity (TENK) guidelines for ethical review in human sciences (https://tenk.fi/sites/default/files/2021-01/Ethical_review_in_human_sciences_2020.pdf), the study did not require formal ethics approval due to its minimal-risk nature. All procedures complied rigorously with TENK principles and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Participation was voluntary, informed consent was mandatory, and data were collected anonymously without retaining any personally identifying information.

Measures

Mood regulation of climate emotions involving music were measured with the Brief Music in Mood Regulation Scale (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?k30y3X which captures seven strategies people use music to influence their emotional state: Entertainment, Revival, Strong Sensation, Diversion, Discharge, Mental Work, and Solace. For the purposes of this study, the instructions were adapted to the climate context by asking participants: "When thoughts or feelings about climate change or environmental crises arise, how do you use music to regulate your emotions?" Participants indicated their agreement with 21 items on a 5-point scale (1 = strongly disagree,5 = strongly agree). Illustrative items include: "Music helps me to understand different feelings in myself" (Mental Work), "When stressful thoughts keep going round and round in my head, I start to listen to music to get them off my mind" (Diversion), "When everything feels bad, music understands and comforts me" (Solace). For the purpose of this study, the overall mean was calculated, with higher scores indicating higher use of music in regulation of climate emotions.

Hope was measured with the Adult Hope Scale (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?2ff7y7 Snyder et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?2ff7y7 1991) , which captures two components of hope: agency (goal-directed determination) and pathways (perceived ability to generate routes toward goals). Respondents indicated their agreement with 12 statements on an 8-point scale from 1 (definitely false) to 8 (definitely true), with higher scores reflecting greater dispositional hope.

Climate efficacy beliefs were measured using four single-item indicators adapted from previous research on efficacy beliefs in the climate crisis (Choi & Hart, 2021; Gregersen et al., 2021). Personal climate self-efficacy was assessed with the question: "How confident are you that you can implement measures to reduce or avoid the impacts of climate change?" Personal outcome expectancy was measured by asking: "How likely is it that your own actions would help reduce climate change?" Collective efficacy was captured with the item: "How likely is it that many people will take measures to try to reduce climate change?" Finally, collective outcome expectancy was assessed by asking: "If large numbers of people implemented such measures, how likely is it that this would reduce climate change?". Each item was rated on an 11-point scale (1 = not at all confident/likely,11 = extremely confident/likely).

Data Analysis

To address the research questions, we first examined pairwise correlations between the music for mood regulation strategies and the outcome measures. Subscale measures were computed as the mean of responses across the items in the sub-scales. Due to the ordinal nature of the data, pairwise correlations were computed with Kendall's tau. Multiple comparison corrections were performed with the Bonferroni method.

Analyses were conducted using the R Statistical language (version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2025) on Windows 11 x64 (build 26200 Participants 366 participants filled the survey at least partially. 1 participant reported being under the age of legal consent (15) and was excluded. 52 participants were missing all responses to the B-MMR scale, efficacy items, and hope scale and were excluded. There were 40 participants missing 1-4 responses so the missing values were imputed with multivariate imputation by chained equations. There were n = 7 participants who failed attention checks. Nonetheless, their data was retained because none of the participants failed both attention checks. Therefore, data from 310 participants was used in the analysis. Their mean age was 36.4 years (SD = 12.4; range = 18-82). Participants had 42 unique nationalities and resided in 38 unique countries. 197 were from developed countries (Europe, North America, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Israel), and 112 were from developing countries. Refer to Table 1 for a summary of the demographic characteristics of the sample.

Results

The data and analyses underlying the results presented herein are available in an Open Science Framework repository (Anonymized view-only link: https://osf.io/j9sdn/overview?view_only=0c7f666fa15a47a1906937c691bae177)

Correlation Analysis

Pairwise correlations were computed with Kendall's tau (see Figure 1). All B-MMR strategies were significantly correlated with the other strategies with the majority of correlations being moderate and strong (τ = .25-.66, p < .001). Similarly, all climate efficacy beliefs were significantly correlated with each other, and all correlations were strong (τ = .33-.56, p < .001).

Some components of climate efficacy were correlated with some B-MMR strategies. Specifically, self-efficacy was positively correlated with solace, diversion, and revival. Personal outcome expectancy showed the same pattern and additionally a positive correlation with music mood regulation for mental work. Collective outcome expectancy was correlated with strategies of solace, mental work, diversion, and strong sensation. No strategies were correlated with collective efficacy.

Hope was significantly correlated with using B-MMR strategies of solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival. When examining the hope subscales separately, agency showed a similar pattern of associations. However, the correlation between agency and solace was not significant, whereas solace was significantly correlated with pathways. Conversely, diversion was significantly correlated with agency but not with pathways.

Measurement Models: Confirmatory Factor Analysis

We assessed the measurement models of each scale with confirmatory factor analyses. The results of the B-MMR were reported in a previous study (Koehler et al., under review) but the sample size in this present study was smaller by one participant therefore we report slightly different results of the B-MMR CFA. Furthermore, missing data in this study was imputed using multivariate chained equations based on the variables included in this study, therefore the imputed missing data in this study may differ from that which was previously reported.

All scales violated the assumption of multivariate normality as assessed with Mardia's test.

Given the ordinal structure of the data and the violation of the multivariate normality assumption, modeling was performed with robust estimators of weighted least squares mean variance (WLSMV). Chi-square tests of measurement model fit were significant for every scale, but the chi-square test is known to be sensitive to sample sizes, therefore we also examined approximate scaled fit indices: the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) with 90% confidence interval, and the Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR). Typical cutoff values for the fit indices are CFI and TLI >= 0.90, RMSEA <= 0.08, and SRMR <= 0.10. We report scaled and robust measures of these fit indices for transparent reporting of the measurement model fits. Fit interpretations are provided in terms of the scaled indices.

The B-MMR was fit with the original structure including the seven subscales each consisting of three items and a higher order general B-MMR structure, but showed inadequate fit and was re-specified to include residual covariance for two similar items on the discharge subscale which then showed adequate fit (see the supplementary material). We evaluated the 2-factor and 1-factor measurement model of the Hope scale and while a latent variable likelihood ratio test indicated that the 2-factor model was a better fit than the 1-factor model, the approximate fit indices were similarly poor for both models, and we chose to use the 1-factor model for several reasons including theoretical justification of interest in a general hope latent variable, and because of the very high correlation between the factors of Agency and Pathways (.935) which makes them virtually indistinguishable. The 1-factor model of Hope was re-specified to include residual covariance for two similar items which then showed improved fit (see the supplementary material). Still, RMSEA was above typical recommendations (scaled RMSEA = 0.110, 95%-CI [0.087, 0.133]; robust RMSEA = 0.096, 95%-CI [0.077, 0.116]). However, RMSEA is sensitive to small degrees of freedom (Kenny et al., 2015) so this measurement model of the Adult Hope Scale was still used in the full measurement model.

Full Measurement Model

The chi-square test of the full measurement model was χ2(367) = 749.63, p = < .001. The scaled incremental fit indices indicated good fit: CFI = 0.969, TLI = 0.965 (robust CFI = 0.885, robust TLI = 0.873). The scaled RMSEA was 0.058 with a 90% confidence interval of [0.052, 0.064], suggesting close approximate fit. However, the robust RMSEA indicates some remaining misfit but the scaled values indicate that the model is appropriate (robust RMSEA = 0.090, 90%-CI [0.083, 0.097]). The SRMR was 0.063, which indicates reasonable fit because it is below the commonly used cutoff of 0.08.

The chi-square test of the structural model was χ2( 475 Figure 2 shows the path diagram of the structural mediation model with both latent and observed variables that are not included in a latent variable. Refer to Table 2 for a summary of the mediation effects. Note that this mediation cannot be used to make causal claims because data was collected cross-sectionally, and these results should be interpreted with that caveat. Music for mood regulation of climate emotions had a significant indirect effect on Hope through self-efficacy (b = 0.049, 95% CI [0.001, 0.104]) and collective efficacy (b = 0.022, 95% CI [0.002, 0.052]), but not through outcome expectancy (b = 0.025, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.076]) or collective outcome expectancy (b = 0.009, 95% CI [-0.023, 0.042]). The total indirect effect was significant (b = 0.105, 95% CI [0.059, 0.158]), and the direct effect remained significant (b = 0.230, 95% CI [0.130, 0.329]), indicating partial mediation. The mediation through self-efficacy and collective efficacy should be interpreted cautiously because these standardized effects are very small. See table 2 for a summary of the Monte Carlo estimated mediation effects.

Discussion

The present study examined whether music-based regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope, and whether this association operates through climate efficacy beliefs. Overall, the findings provide evidence that individuals who report greater use of music to regulate climate-related emotions also report higher levels of hope. Furthermore, climate efficacy beliefs partly accounted for this association, although not all efficacy dimensions played an equally important role. These findings suggest that music may support adaptive engagement with climate-related emotions in ways that extend beyond immediate emotional relief and may contribute to psychological resources associated with coping with environmental challenges.

Consistent with H1, music-based mood regulation of climate emotions was positively associated with hope. At the bivariate level, several specific regulation strategies, particularly solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival, showed positive associations with hope. These findings align with broader literature demonstrating that music can facilitate emotional coping, provide comfort during challenging circumstances, and foster positive emotional experiences (Koehler et al., 2023; Saarikallio et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2013). While most previous work has examined music's role in regulating general emotions, the present findings suggest that similar processes may be relevant when individuals confront climate-related distress. Music may help individuals tolerate difficult climate emotions without becoming overwhelmed by them, thereby creating psychological conditions that support the maintenance of hope (Ziv et al., 2011). Notably, the strategies associated with hope were those that involve seeking emotional comfort (solace), temporarily distancing oneself from distressing thoughts (diversion), restoring energy and vitality (revival), or intensifying meaningful emotional experiences (strong sensation). This suggests that hope may be supported not only by reducing negative affect but also by providing diverse psychological resources that help individuals remain psychologically engaged in the climate crisis.

Regarding the relationships between musical regulation of climate emotions and climate efficacy beliefs (H2), our findings revealed that some music-based regulation strategies were positively associated with self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, and collective outcome expectancy, whereas no significant correlations emerged between regulation strategies and collective efficacy. Consistent with previous research on different psychological functions of climate efficacy beliefs (Hamann et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?aezPNg 2024) , our findings also suggest that not all efficacy beliefs are equally connected to how people use music in the context of climate emotions. The strongest pattern emerged for beliefs about one's own ability to respond effectively to climate change, whereas associations with beliefs about collective action were less consistent. One interpretation is that music-based regulation primarily operates at the level of individual emotional experience and may therefore be more closely linked to perceptions of personal capability than to broader judgments about societal action.

Concerning the mediation hypothesis (H3), our results showed that the overall indirect effect of music-based regulation on hope through climate efficacy beliefs was significant, indicating that efficacy beliefs constitute one pathway connecting music-based regulation and hope. However, only self-efficacy and collective efficacy emerged as significant mediators. Outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy did not significantly mediate the relationship. This differential pattern across efficacy beliefs may provide insight into the mechanisms through which music-based regulation is associated with hope.

According to social cognitive theory (Bandurahttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?CyyERQ 1986) , efficacy beliefs reflect perceptions of capability ("Can I/we do something?"), whereas outcome expectancies reflect beliefs about whether actions will be effective ("Will it make a difference?"). Researchers have argued that these constructs should be distinguished rather than treated as a single form of efficacy (Choi, 2026). Music may be particularly well suited to supporting feelings of agency and capability by helping individuals manage difficult climate emotions, sustain engagement with climate issues, and avoid becoming overwhelmed. In contrast, music may have less influence on beliefs about the likely effectiveness of climate action, which may depend more heavily on perceptions of political, social, and environmental realities. From this perspective, music-based regulation may promote hope primarily by strengthening people's sense that they can respond to the climate crisis, rather than by increasing confidence that climate actions will necessarily succeed.

Our findings are consistent with previous research positioning efficacy beliefs as central psychological resources for coping with environmental threats (Hurst Loo & Walker, 2023; Li & Monroe, 2019; Ojala, 2012). The mediation through collective efficacy was somewhat unexpected given the absence of significant bivariate correlations between the individual mood-regulation strategies and collective efficacy. One explanation is that collective efficacy may become relevant only when considering overall music-based mood regulation as a latent construct rather than individual strategies in isolation. Structural equation modeling accounts for shared variance across indicators and corrects for measurement error, potentially revealing relationships that are not evident at the observed-variable level. Further, the direct association between musical regulation and hope remained significant after accounting for all efficacy beliefs, indicating partial rather than full mediation. Although the indirect effects were statistically significant, their magnitude was small, suggesting that efficacy beliefs explain only a limited portion of the association between music-based regulation and hope. This suggests that music may foster hope through additional mechanisms beyond cognitive pathways such as climate efficacy beliefs. For examplehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?FCIn1v music may provide emotional meaninghttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7KIcO7 support self-awareness and reinforce social connectedness (Schäfer et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?V2AQf5 2013) , support identity processes (Ørjasæter et al., 2017) , or evoke positive affective states (Ziv et al., 2011) , that contribute directly to hopeful thinking. Hope may therefore arise not only from cognitive beliefs about effectiveness and agency but also from experiential and emotional processes supported by musical engagement.

The present findings have several implications for research on climate emotions and psychological adaptation to climate change. First, they extend the literature on music and emotion regulation into the context of climate-related distress, suggesting that music may function not only as a tool for managing difficult emotions but also as a resource for sustaining hope in the face of environmental change. While climate emotion research has increasingly focused on identifying adaptive coping resources (Ágoston et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?8CBMbu 2022; Crandon et al., 2024) , musical engagement has received relatively little attention despite being a highly accessible and widely used everyday practice. Second, the findings suggest that music may contribute to climate adaptation primarily by supporting feelings of agency rather than shaping beliefs about the effectiveness of climate action. By helping individuals regulate difficult climate emotions and remain engaged, music may support the psychological capacity to act and persist in the face of environmental crisis, which may be especially important when confronting a complex and often overwhelming issue such as climate change. More broadly, the results corroborate previous theoretical research (Ibrahim, 2024) that cultural and emotional practices may play an important role in supporting psychological adaptation to climate change. In addition to policyhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?v96x3i education, and communication interventions, everyday resources that are already embedded in daily life, such as music (Feneberg et al., 2025) , may help individuals remain emotionally engaged with climate challenges while maintaining a sense of hope and possibility for the future.

Limitations and Future Directions

This study has several limitations. First, its cross-sectional design prevents inferences about temporal ordering or causality, and future experimental or longitudinal work is needed to clarify directionality among music-based regulation of climate emotions, climate efficacy beliefs, and wellbeing. Further, the observed indirect effects through self-efficacy and collective efficacy were statistically significant but small. These findings suggest that efficacy beliefs explain only a modest proportion of the association between music-based regulation and hope. Future research should therefore investigate additional mediating mechanisms, such as meaning-making, emotional resilience, social connectedness, identity processes, or climate-related collective action, that may more fully account for how musical engagement contributes to hope in the context of climate change. Second, we did not control for potentially relevant third variables-such as personality traits, environmental activism, general music listening habits, or broader emotion-regulation tendencies-which may influence both music use and psychological outcomes. Third, the adapted measure of music-based mood regulation referred broadly to climate-related emotions, a category that spans diverse positive and negative states; however, we did not assess which specific emotions participants were regulating (e.g., anger, anxiety, worry, hope), nor did we capture contextual features of musical engagement (e.g., listening situations, genre, or mode of interaction). Future research could examine whether different forms of musical engagement are particularly effective for regulating specific climate emotions and fostering hope. Fourth, although recruitment included multiple channels, the sample may not be fully representative of the broader population, and online survey participation may select for individuals with higher digital literacy or stronger interest in climate issues. Finally, single-item indicators were used to assess efficacy beliefs; while common in this literature, they may offer less precision than multi-item scales. Similarly, although the Adult Hope Scale was selected because of its extensive use and strong theoretical foundation, alternative instruments developed specifically for environmental or climate-related contexts may capture hope about the climate crisis more directly. Future research could therefore benefit from employing multi-item measures of climate efficacy beliefs and comparing different conceptualizations of climate-related constructs to assess the robustness of the observed associations.

Conclusion

The present study provides initial evidence that music-based regulation of climate emotions is associated with greater hope in the face of the climate crisis. Climate efficacy beliefs partially explained this relationship, particularly self-efficacy and collective efficacy, although most of the association remained direct. These findings suggest that music may support not only the regulation of difficult climate emotions but also provide psychological resources that help individuals remain hopeful and engaged. As societies seek effective ways to cope with the emotional consequences of climate change, everyday cultural practices such as music may represent an important and largely overlooked source of psychological adaptation.
